Where is Eugene, Oregon, and how is the city laid out?

Eugene is the county seat of Lane County, at the southern end of the Willamette Valley, close to where the McKenzie and Willamette rivers meet. It sits about 110 miles south of Portland and about 50 miles east of the Oregon coast.

The city is divided into 23 neighborhoods, from Whiteaker, Downtown and the two University districts near campus to River Road, Santa Clara, Cal Young, Churchill, Bethel, Far West and the Southwest Hills. Skinner Butte, Spencer Butte and Mount Pisgah give the area its hills, and Amazon Creek runs through town. A hillside lot near Spencer Butte and a house on flat ground in a neighborhood such as Trainsong or Harlow present different repair and access questions.

What is the history of Eugene?

Eugene Skinner built the first pioneer cabin on Skinner's Butte in 1846, and the settlement was named Eugene City in 1853. The cabin became a trading post and an official post office on January 8, 1850.

The town incorporated on October 17, 1862 and dropped the word City in 1889. The University of Oregon was created by the Legislature in 1872 and enrolled its first students on October 16, 1876. Eugene adopted a council and manager form of government in 1944.

Who are the biggest employers in Eugene?

Health care and education lead. The city's 2017 annual financial report lists these five employers, as summarized on Wikipedia:

  • PeaceHealth Medical Group: 5,808 employees
  • University of Oregon: 5,549
  • Eugene School District 4J: 2,553
  • U.S. Government: 1,750
  • Lane Community College: 1,650

Wood products and recreational vehicle manufacturing are the largest industries, and Bi-Mart and Market of Choice are headquartered here. Lane County reports tourism spending of $1.1 billion in 2023. A job change can push an owner to sell on a short timeline.

How does Eugene's climate affect a house?

Eugene is wet in winter and mild overall, with 40.83 inches of precipitation in an average year and about 7.1 inches of snow. The average annual temperature is 53.1 degrees Fahrenheit.

Moisture is the main wear factor for a Eugene home: roofs, gutters, crawl spaces, siding and decks all take a beating from the long damp season. The weather can also swing the other way. Eugene hit 111 degrees on June 27, 2021, and the record low is minus 12 degrees from December 8, 1972.

Wildfire is a regional concern. The 2020 Holiday Farm Fire burned 173,393 acres in the McKenzie River valley in Lane County between September 7 and October 29, 2020, and many people evacuated to nearby Springfield.

Which school districts serve Eugene?

Eugene School District 4J covers about 85% of the city limits and runs four full-service high schools: Churchill, North Eugene, Sheldon and South Eugene. Bethel School District serves the northwest edge of the city and includes 11 schools.

Higher education includes the University of Oregon, Bushnell University, Lane Community College and a Pacific University campus. Students and faculty create a rental market near campus, and a house's district boundary is one of the first things a buyer's agent checks.

How do roads and transit shape Eugene housing?

Interstate 5 forms much of Eugene's eastern edge, and Oregon Route 99 is the main surface artery through town. Eugene Airport (Mahlon Sweet Field) is the second-largest airport in Oregon.

  • Lane Transit District, formed in 1970, covers 240 square miles and carries about 3.7 million trips per year.
  • The EmX bus rapid transit line links Eugene and Springfield.
  • The restored 1908 depot downtown is the southern end of two daily Amtrak Cascades trips.

Houses along the EmX corridor and near downtown appeal to people without a car, while hillside and far west properties depend more on driving.

What utilities serve a Eugene house?

The Eugene Water & Electric Board provides both electricity and water to more than 86,000 customers in and around Eugene. It was founded in 1911, is chartered by the city and is governed by an elected five-member board. A seller can ask EWEB about closing or transferring service before the sale date.

What rules apply if I own a rental house in Eugene?

Rental units in Eugene, including rooms for rent, must be registered with the city's Rental Housing Program, and owners must name an emergency contact who lives within 75 miles. The code applies only inside city limits, even if a property has a Eugene mailing address.

  • Rent increases above the state maximum require at least 90 days' notice and relocation assistance equal to two months of rent.
  • Tenants must give written notice before filing a complaint, and the owner then has 10 days to fix a problem (48 hours for essential services).
  • Owners must notify the program when they sell a unit.

An owner who inherits or tires of managing a rental should sort out registration, any open complaints and the tenant's move-out timing before setting a closing date. Details come from the city's Landlord Handbook.

When are property taxes due in Lane County?

Oregon tax statements are mailed by October 25, and you can pay all at once or in three equal parts due November 15, February 15 and May 15. Paying the full amount by November 15 earns a 3% discount, and paying two-thirds by then earns 2%.

Late installments accrue interest at 1.333% per month. If a due date falls on a weekend or holiday it moves to the next business day. Measure 50, approved by voters in 1997, replaced the earlier Measure 47 and applies the 3% limit to assessed value. Lane County collects the tax for Eugene, and a seller should confirm the payoff status with the title company before closing.

What must an Oregon seller disclose?

Under ORS 105.464, a seller of covered residential property must give the buyer a written disclosure statement once the buyer makes a written offer. The form asks about title and boundaries, water and sewage, structure, systems, seismic issues, flooding, settling and other known defects.

A buyer has five days after getting the form to revoke the offer unless they waived that right. Exclusions exist, for example for sales by a court-appointed personal representative or by a bank after foreclosure. The form relies on the seller's actual knowledge, so answer honestly, and note that it contains no "as is" language.

What do sellers in Eugene usually face?

  • Older homes with deferred roof, moisture or sewer-line work after years of wet winters.
  • Inherited houses where several family members must agree and probate or a trust must be settled first.
  • Rental houses with tenants, registration paperwork and relocation rules to follow.
  • A student-driven calendar near the university, where timing around the school year changes how fast a house moves.
  • Owners behind on payments who want a certain closing date.

When condition or timing is the problem, many Eugene owners compare a traditional listing against a direct cash sale. A cash buyer purchases the house in its current state, so repairs, showings and buyer financing drop out of the picture. We buy houses in Eugene as they are, and you can request an offer online or by phone.

More questions about Eugene, OR

Does Eugene have a transfer tax on home sales?

The county transfer tax in Washington County is set by that county's own code, Chapter 3.04. We could not confirm from an official page whether Lane County has any similar charge, so ask the title or escrow company to confirm what applies to a Eugene sale. Title, escrow and recording charges still apply and are set by the companies and the county clerk.

What is Eugene's population?

The Census Bureau counted 176,654 residents in the 2020 Census, and the Bureau's estimate for July 1, 2025 is 178,618.

Do I need to register a rental house before selling it in Eugene?

Yes, if it is a rental inside city limits, it should be registered with the Rental Housing Program, and the program expects to be told when a unit is sold. Ask the city if you are unsure of a unit's status.

How long do Eugene property tax installments run?

Oregon bills in three parts due November 15, February 15 and May 15, with a 3% discount for paying in full by November 15. Interest of 1.333% per month applies after each due date.

Can I sell a Eugene house with tenants living in it?

Yes, the sale is possible, but the tenant's lease and Oregon and Eugene notice rules continue to apply. Talk to a landlord-tenant attorney if move-out timing is part of the plan.

Where is Gresham, Oregon?

Gresham is a city in Multnomah County that borders Portland on its northwest side, on the eastern edge of the Portland metro area. It covers roughly 23 square miles, with hills along the eastern border and a hilly northeast where it meets Troutdale near the Columbia River.

Johnson Creek runs west through the city, and about 23% of its watershed lies in Gresham. Multnomah County is the smallest county in Oregon by area at about 466 square miles, yet it is also the most populous, with 815,428 residents in 2020. Neighboring cities include Troutdale, Fairview and Wood Village.

How did Gresham begin?

Brothers Jackson and James Powell settled the area in 1851 under the Donation Land Claim Act and called it Powell's Valley. In 1884 a merchant proposed the name Gresham for a post office, honoring Walter Quintin Gresham, a Civil War general and U.S. Secretary of State.

Gresham incorporated on February 11, 1905, when it had 365 residents. Raspberries, grapes and vegetables were the main crops from the 1910s to the 1960s. The population was 3,944 in 1960 and 90,205 in 2000, a rise of more than 20-fold in four decades. Gresham General Hospital opened in 1959 and moved to Stark Street in 1984 as Mount Hood Medical Center.

Which neighborhoods make up Gresham?

Gresham has 16 recognized neighborhoods: Central City, Centennial, Gresham Butte, Historic Southeast, Hogan Cedars, Hollybrook, Kelly Creek, North Central, North Gresham, Northeast, Northwest, Pleasant Valley, Powell Valley, Rockwood, Southwest and Wilkes East.

The city's trail network includes the Springwater Corridor, the 40-Mile Loop and the Gresham-Fairview Trail, and Main City Park sits near downtown.

What does the Gresham economy look like?

Gresham is described as the economic center for eastern Multnomah County, and it grew from a farming town into a city of more than 100,000. Mount Hood Medical Center, which opened as Gresham General Hospital in 1959, and the community college are anchors in town.

Countywide, major industries include manufacturing, transportation, wholesale and retail trade and tourism, and the Port of Portland is a significant West Coast shipping hub. About 27% of Gresham residents hold a bachelor's degree, according to Census figures cited by Wikipedia.

Which school districts serve Gresham?

Three districts serve the city: Centennial, Gresham-Barlow and Reynolds. High schools include Gresham, Sam Barlow, Springwater Trail, Centennial and Reynolds, and Mount Hood Community College is in Gresham.

Because the city is split among three districts, the address matters. Two houses a few blocks apart can feed different schools, and sellers should be ready to tell buyers which district a property belongs to.

How do I get around Gresham?

  • Interstate 84 provides western access, and U.S. Route 26 provides eastern access.
  • TriMet buses and the MAX Blue Line light rail serve the city, with the Blue Line's eastern end at Cleveland Avenue.
  • The fareless Sandy Area Metro shuttle connects Gresham to Sandy.

Gresham sits at the eastern end of the Portland metro transit network, which matters to commuters weighing a house here against one closer in.

What does Gresham's weather mean for a house?

Gresham has a Mediterranean climate with wet winters and dry summers, and December is the wettest month at 7.61 inches of rain. The mean daily high is 82 degrees in July and August and 46 degrees in January, and the average low in January is 35 degrees.

That much winter rain keeps pressure on roofs, gutters, siding and crawl spaces. Snow is light at 5.8 inches a year, with relative humidity averaging 75%.

How is Gresham governed, and what landmarks does it have?

Gresham uses a council and manager form of government, with a mayor and six councilors who serve four-year terms. The city manager, Eric Schmidt, was appointed in June 2024.

Historic sites include the Gresham Carnegie Library, built in 1913, and the Jacob Zimmerman House, built in 1874, both on the National Register of Historic Places. Gresham Pioneer Cemetery was founded in 1859. Mount Hood Community College, in Gresham, offers associate degrees and bachelor's programs through a partnership with Eastern Oregon University.

Can I add or rent out an accessory dwelling unit in Gresham?

Gresham allows accessory dwelling units, which the city caps by size, and renting one requires a residential rental license. Short-term rentals, including bed and breakfasts, are prohibited in an ADU.

  • Conversions or ADUs attached to the house: up to 900 square feet.
  • ADUs beside or behind a garage: up to 750 square feet, including the garage.
  • Freestanding ADUs: 750 square feet or 50% of the house size, whichever is less.
  • Three paved on-site parking spaces, each 8.5 feet by 18 feet.

Simple conversions go through Type I review in about two to three weeks, while attached additions that enlarge the footprint and most freestanding units go through Type II review that takes roughly three to four months. An existing ADU without permits can complicate a sale, so confirm its status with the city planner.

When are Multnomah County property taxes due?

Oregon statements go out by October 25, and the three installments are due November 15, February 15 and May 15. Pay in full by November 15 to save 3%, or pay two-thirds to save 2%.

Interest on a late installment runs at 1.333% per month, starting December 16, February 16 or May 16. Taxes under $40 cannot be split. Oregon Measure 50 was approved on May 20, 1997, and replaced Measure 47. Ask the title company for the current payoff and any unpaid installments before closing.

What must a Gresham seller tell the buyer?

Oregon sellers of covered residential property must give each buyer who submits a written offer a signed disclosure statement under ORS 105.464. It asks about title, water, sewage, structure, systems, flooding, settling and other defects, and the buyer has five days to revoke the offer unless they waived that right.

Exclusions include a sale by a personal representative, trustee or conservator and a bank sale after foreclosure. The form relies on what the seller actually knows, so list problems you are aware of instead of leaving them blank.

What do Gresham sellers usually face?

  • Houses from the suburban building boom that need roof, window or drainage updates.
  • Inherited homes in neighborhoods such as Rockwood or Historic Southeast, where heirs live elsewhere.
  • Landlords with tenants in a house they no longer want to manage.
  • Owners with unpermitted ADUs or garage conversions.
  • Homeowners behind on payments who want certainty on timing.

A cash sale lets an owner skip repairs and showings. We buy houses in Gresham in their current condition, and the offer request takes only a few minutes.

The Census Bureau counted 114,247 residents in 2020, and its July 1, 2025 estimate is 111,513. Gresham is the fourth largest city in Oregon.

Does Multnomah County charge a transfer tax on home sales?

Washington County sets its own transfer tax under its county code, Chapter 3.04. We could not confirm an official Multnomah County transfer tax, so ask the title or escrow company what applies to a Gresham sale. Closing costs for title and escrow still apply.

When is the first Oregon property tax installment due?

November 15. The other two are due February 15 and May 15, and a 3% discount applies to full payment by November 15.

Can a Gresham house be sold if it has an unpermitted ADU?

It can be sold, but the buyer may ask about permits and the city treats ADUs under specific size, parking and review rules. Speak with the city's Planner on Duty if the status is unclear.

Which school district is my Gresham house in?

It depends on the address. Gresham is served by the Centennial, Gresham-Barlow and Reynolds districts, so check the district's boundary map for the exact property.

Where is Medford, Oregon, and what is the land like?

Medford is the county seat of Jackson County, in the Rogue Valley about 27 miles north of the California border. It sits at 1,434 feet in a rain shadow between the Cascade Range and the Siskiyou Mountains, which explains the dry summers.

Roxy Ann Peak rises to 3,576 feet at the edge of town, and Prescott Park around it covers 1,740 acres. Bear Creek Park runs nearly 100 acres, and Alba Park, deeded to the city in 1888, is the oldest. Houses on the foothills and houses on the valley floor face different slopes, drainage and fire exposure, so describe the lot as well as the building.

How did Medford get its start?

Medford began as a railroad survey stop. Surveyors working on the Oregon and California Railroad route in 1883 included David Loring, who named the town for Medford, Massachusetts.

  • The town was platted in early December 1883 with 82 blocks.
  • The first post office opened February 6, 1884.
  • Medford incorporated as a town on February 24, 1885, and as a city in 1905.
  • It took the county seat from Jacksonville in 1927.
  • Interstate 5 was completed through town in 1967.

That timeline matters for sellers because it explains the mix of old railroad-era streets near downtown and newer subdivisions farther out.

What does Medford's population look like?

Medford is the eighth-largest city in Oregon and the largest in Jackson County. The 2020 census counted 85,824 residents, and the Census Bureau estimates 86,494 as of July 1, 2025.

Which employers drive the Medford economy?

Health care is the largest driver. Asante Rogue Regional Medical Center and Providence Medford Medical Center together employ more than 2,000 people.

  • Harry and David is described as the largest employer in Southern Oregon, with about 1,700 year-round and 6,700 seasonal workers.
  • Lithia Motors, a Fortune 500 company, has been headquartered in Medford since 1970.
  • Jackson County has more than 10,000 acres of orchards and shares the Rogue Valley and Applegate wine appellations with Josephine County.

With seasonal work at Harry and David and shift work in health care, a rental's tenant mix can turn over on a different calendar than a typical house, so check lease end dates before you set a closing date.

How hot and dry does Medford get, and what does that do to a house?

Medford has a Mediterranean climate with hot summers and dry air. Summers average 61 afternoons above 90 degrees and 11 above 100, and the record high is 115 degrees, reached July 20, 1946 and again June 28, 2021.

Annual precipitation averages 18.43 inches and snowfall 3.4 inches. Winter temperature inversions can hold fog in the valley for weeks. Long hot spells age roofing, exterior paint and air conditioning equipment, and a buyer's inspector will look at all three.

How did the Almeda fire affect Medford housing?

The Almeda fire started the morning of September 8, 2020, and swept through the Rogue Valley within hours. Jefferson Public Radio reported more than 2,600 homes destroyed between Ashland, Talent, Phoenix and Medford, calling it the most destructive wildfire in Oregon's recorded history.

Medford lost homes too, including a mobile home park in the city. A year later, thousands of displaced residents had not received the federal help they needed to rebuild. For a seller, the effects show up in two ways:

  • Under ORS 308.146, a fire or other act of God that cuts a property's real market value also reduces its maximum assessed value for that year.

Where is Grants Pass, Oregon?

Grants Pass is the county seat of Josephine County, on Interstate 5 along the Rogue River in southern Oregon's Rogue Valley, northwest of Medford. The city sits at about 960 feet of elevation and covers roughly 11 square miles.

Josephine County itself is large, at 1,642 square miles and 88,090 residents in the 2020 Census. Most of the land belongs to the federal government: the Forest Service owns about 39% and the Bureau of Land Management about 28%. That is why many homes here sit next to public forest rather than farmland.

How did Grants Pass get its name and start?

The city says its name honors Ulysses S. Grant's success in the Vicksburg Campaign. Fur trappers passed through from the 1820s along the Siskiyou Trail, and settlers on the Applegate Trail came through in the late 1840s.

The post office opened on March 22, 1865, and the city incorporated in 1887. Voters moved the county seat here from Kerby in an 1886 vote. The Caveman Bridge on 6th Street, designed by Conde McCullough, dates from 1933 and was refurbished in 2019.

A sugar beet factory opened in 1916, but its processing machinery moved to Toppenish, Washington around 1918 and 1919. The Rogue River itself remains the city's defining feature, and the area's hot-summer Mediterranean climate fits USDA hardiness zone 8b. Population grew from 23,003 in 2000 to 34,533 in 2010 and 39,189 in 2020, a 13.5% rise in the last decade.

What drives the Grants Pass economy?

Lumber was the major employer until the early 1970s, then automation and federal timber cuts drove a long decline. At least 20 sawmill, veneer and plywood mills in Jackson, Josephine and Curry counties closed after 1980, and the 1994 Northwest Forest Plan set federal harvests roughly 70% below 1970s levels.

  • Outdoor recreation, including guided Rogue River fishing and boat trips
  • Health care and small and medium businesses
  • Dutch Bros coffee, founded in Grants Pass in 1992 (headquarters moved to Arizona in 2025)
  • The Boatnik hydroplane race on Memorial Day weekend and the Josephine County Fair in late August

The metro area's gross domestic product was $3.877 billion in 2023.

What is the Grants Pass climate like, and how does it affect houses?

Grants Pass has hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters, with about 31 inches of precipitation a year and roughly three quarters of it falling between November 1 and March 31. The August average high is 90.6 degrees, and the city averages about 51 afternoons a year at or above 90 degrees and 8 at or above 100.

The record high is 115 degrees, set on July 4, 2022. Snow is light.

Wildfire smoke and fire risk are part of life in southwest Oregon. In July 2025 the Board Shanty Fire grew to 409 acres south of Grants Pass and triggered Level 2 evacuation notices in several Josephine County zones, according to the Grants Pass Tribune.

What is there to see in Grants Pass?

Riverside Park hosts Boatnik and the Concerts in the Park series, and the Cathedral Hills Trail System, maintained by the Bureau of Land Management, includes the largest whiteleaf manzanita in Oregon. The downtown Rogue Theatre is now a performing arts venue.

The Grants Pass post office has two 1938 New Deal murals, the only Oregon post office with two. The city's motto is "It's the Climate." The council has eight members across four wards who serve four-year terms, and the mayor is Clint Scherf.

Which schools and colleges serve Grants Pass?

The Grants Pass School District serves the city, including Grants Pass High School. Three Rivers School District includes Illinois Valley High, North Valley High, Rivers Edge Academy Charter School and Hidden Valley High.

Rogue Community College's Redwood Campus is just south of the city, with other campuses in Medford and White City.

How do roads connect Grants Pass?

Interstate 5 runs through the area, and U.S. Route 199 passes through the city and joins I-5. The Redwood Highway runs south of the city toward California. For a seller, freeway access is a selling point for commuters to the Medford area, while rural properties on private roads face their own questions.

What are the rules for vacation rentals in Grants Pass?

Grants Pass regulates vacation rental dwellings under Sections 14.800 to 14.840 of its development code, and a Director-issued permit and a Title 4 license are required before a unit is advertised. Only single-family dwellings and existing accessory dwelling units are eligible.

  • Stays are limited to 27 days in any 30-day period.
  • Overnight occupancy is two people per sleeping room plus two more, capped at 12.
  • Parking is two cars in the driveway and one on the street.
  • The transient room tax applies, and a guest register must be kept.

An owner who inherits a house run as a vacation rental should confirm the permit status before listing it.

What did the U.S. Supreme Court decide about Grants Pass?

In City of Grants Pass v. Johnson, decided June 28, 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that cities may enforce public camping bans even without enough shelter space. The case was brought against the City of Grants Pass.

When are Josephine County property taxes due?

Property tax statements in Oregon are mailed by October 25, with installments due November 15, February 15 and May 15. A 3% discount applies when the full amount is paid by November 15, and 2% when two thirds is paid.

Late payments accrue interest at 1.333% per month. Josephine County has had budget strain: voters rejected a $12 million levy in November 2014, which led to 70 layoffs and the release of about 90 jail inmates.

What must a Grants Pass seller disclose?

Oregon law, ORS 105.464, requires a seller of covered residential property to give each buyer who makes a written offer a disclosure statement covering water, sewage, structure, systems, flooding, settling and other known defects. The buyer has five days to revoke unless that right was waived.

Sales by court-appointed personal representatives, trustees and conservators, and bank sales after foreclosure, can claim an exclusion.

Where is Oregon City, and why does its terrain matter?

Oregon City is the county seat of Clackamas County, on the Willamette River near the southern edge of the Portland metro area. The city sits at 466 feet and is built in two tiers: a lower area on a bench beside the river and an upper area on a basalt bluff.

The Willamette forms the boundary with West Linn, and the Clackamas River forms the boundary with Gladstone. A water-powered elevator linked the two tiers in 1915, was converted to electricity in the 1920s and replaced by a new electric elevator in 1952. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. If your house is on the bluff, say so, since buyers care about slope, views and walking access.

Which Oregon City neighborhoods come up most?

The city lists 12 official neighborhood associations. Three areas stand out in descriptions of the city.

  • McLoughlin sits on the bluff above downtown and has many older homes, the McLoughlin House, the public library, a pool and a hospital.
  • Canemah is a narrow strip between the Willamette and a bluff along OR 99E. It was founded in 1845 as an independent city, served as the portage site around the falls, and was later annexed.
  • Two Rivers is the lowest part of the city and mostly commercial, including downtown and Clackamette Park.

What is Oregon City's history?

Oregon City was the end of the Oregon Trail and the first U.S. city west of the Rocky Mountains to incorporate. Dr. John McLoughlin of the Hudson's Bay Company founded the settlement in 1829 to use Willamette Falls to power a lumber mill, and the city incorporated in 1844.

  • It was the capital of Oregon Territory from 1848 to 1851.
  • The Oregon Spectator, published in 1846, was the first American newspaper west of the Rockies.
  • In 1889 the city began the first long-distance electrical service in the country, sending power 14 miles to Portland.
  • The Willamette Falls Locks, in West Linn, were the first multi-lift navigational locks in the U.S.

What does the Oregon City economy rely on?

Forestry dominated the city's history until the Pacific Northwest lumber industry declined starting in the 1980s, and today Oregon City is largely a Portland suburb. The last paper mill in the immediate area closed in 2017 and reopened in 2019 under new ownership.

Tourism built on history is growing, centered on the Willamette Falls Legacy Project, a planned public-access, mixed-use redevelopment of the falls area. Clackamas Community College is in the city. The End of the Oregon Trail Interpretive Center closed in September 2009 over funding and reopened in summer 2013. Other sites include the Museum of the Oregon Territory, the 1908 Stevens-Crawford Heritage House Museum, the Ermatinger House, the oldest in Clackamas County, and the 1922 Oregon City Bridge.

What does the weather mean for an Oregon City house?

Oregon City has hot, dry summers and cool, wet winters, with most of its 44.81 inches of annual rain falling from November to March. The annual average temperature is 55.4 degrees, and December averages 41.8.

The record high is 114 degrees, set June 28, 2021, and the record low is minus 2, on January 31, 1950. A wet half of the year is hard on roofs, decks and retaining walls, and bluff lots add drainage to the list of things a buyer will check.

How do roads, trains and buses serve Oregon City?

Interstate 205 crosses the northern edge of the city and is the only freeway serving it. Oregon Routes 43, 99E and 213 pass through or end in town.

  • Amtrak Cascades trains stop twice daily in each direction between Portland and Eugene, while the Coast Starlight passes without stopping.
  • TriMet buses converge at the Oregon City Transit Center, with added service from South Clackamas Transportation District and Canby Area Transit.
  • There is no public airport in the city. Portland International is about 15 miles north.

Which schools serve Oregon City?

The Oregon City School District has seven elementary schools, two middle schools, Oregon City High School and an alternative secondary school. Several schools offer bilingual English and Spanish programs. Oregon City High School is described as the third most populated high school in Oregon.

What do Oregon City historic districts mean for a seller?

McMinnville began with a land claim. William T. Newby claimed the site in 1844, built a grist mill in 1853, and platted the town on May 5, 1856, naming it for his hometown of McMinnville, Tennessee. The plat was not recorded until July 1865.

Where is Forest Grove, Oregon?

Forest Grove is a city in Washington County, about 25 miles west of Portland in the Tualatin Valley, on the western edge of the Portland metro area. It covers about six square miles at an elevation near 190 feet.

Washington County is Oregon's second most populous county, with 600,372 residents in 2020, and Hillsboro is the county seat. The northern and western parts of the county are forested, and the fertile plain around Forest Grove drew farmers early on.

How did Forest Grove begin?

The Atfalati band of the Kalapuya people lived on the Tualatin Plains before Euro-American settlement. Alvin T. and Abigail Smith settled in 1841, and Smith became the first postmaster on February 1, 1850, with his log cabin serving as the post office.

Trustees of Tualatin Academy, later Pacific University, chose the name on January 10, 1851, after a grove of oak trees on the campus. Forest Grove incorporated in 1872, the first city in Washington County. Rail service arrived with the Oregon Electric in November 1908 and the Southern Pacific in January 1914. Red Electric passenger service ended in 1929 and the Oregon Electric stopped running in 1932.

The city counted 547 people in 1880, 1,772 in 1910, 17,708 in 2000 and 21,083 in 2010. The 2020 Census count of 26,225 means about 5,000 more residents in ten years, and 99.7% of residents live in urban areas. Washington County's electronics growth in the 1980s and 1990s helped create what people call Oregon's Silicon Forest.

Nyuzen, Japan is Forest Grove's sister city, and the city's motto is "A place where families and businesses thrive."

Chemawa Indian School opened in Forest Grove in 1880 and moved to Salem in 1884. The fire department started in 1894. Median age is 35.3, and 23.5% of residents are under 18.

What is the farmland and geography around Forest Grove?

Most of Washington County lies in the Tualatin Valley, which the Tualatin River flows through, and the county's highest point is South Saddle Mountain at 3,464 feet. Agriculture remains a major industry alongside lumber, manufacturing and food processing.

A 1997 count found orchards on 8,403 acres and vineyards on 1,163 acres across the county. That farm and orchard base is part of why the area west of Hillsboro still has a rural edge.

Forest Grove has a warm-summer Mediterranean climate, with 46.72 inches of precipitation a year across about 146 days with measurable precipitation. No average monthly temperature exceeds 71.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

Extremes do happen: the record high is 113 degrees in June and the record low is minus 12 degrees. Snow averages only 2.7 inches. The damp winters are the main factor for roofs, siding, gutters and crawl spaces on older houses.

Forest Grove has two historic districts, the Clark Historic District and Painter's Woods, plus 12 individually listed properties on the National Register of Historic Places. The Clark district spans 18 blocks and includes homes dating to 1854.

An older house inside or near a historic area often carries original windows, old wiring and plumbing.

Forest Grove Light & Power, a city-owned utility founded in 1895, supplies electricity. It is the third-oldest municipal electric utility in Oregon.

A seller should call before the closing date to transfer or stop service.

Tuality Forest Grove Hospital is also in the city.

How do roads and buses serve Forest Grove?

  • Oregon Route 8, the Tualatin Valley Highway, and Oregon Route 47 are the main highways.
  • TriMet and the Yamhill County Transit Area run buses.
  • Ride Connection's free GroveLink service covers parts of the city.

Forest Grove is primarily a commuter town for the Portland metro area. Washington County's electronics industry, centered in Hillsboro, is a large regional employer: Intel has its biggest local presence there, and Nike's headquarters is also in the county.

Oregon tax statements are mailed by October 25, and installments are due November 15, February 15 and May 15. Full payment by November 15 earns a 3% discount, and two thirds earns 2%.

Interest on late payments is 1.333% per month. Taxes under $40 cannot be paid in installments. Measure 50 passed in 1997 and replaced Measure 47. A title company will show any unpaid installments before closing.

Under ORS 105.464, a seller of covered residential property must give each buyer who submits a written offer a signed disclosure statement covering title, water, sewage, structure, systems, flooding, settling and other known defects. A buyer has five days to revoke unless they waived that right.

Exclusions apply to sales by a personal representative, trustee or conservator, and to bank sales after foreclosure.

Newberg has cool, wet winters and warm, dry summers. July is the warmest month with an average high of 80.0 degrees, while December and January highs average 46.

Rain averages 39.95 inches a year over about 152 days. Freezing temperatures occur on about 33 nights a year, with snow mainly from December through March. The record high is 107 degrees and the record low is minus 3. Water in crawl spaces, gutters that overflow, and pipes in unheated areas are the usual trouble spots for older houses here.

How do highways and the bypass affect Newberg buyers?

Oregon Route 99W runs east to west through Newberg, linking Portland to the northeast with Dundee and McMinnville to the southwest. For years that single road carried severe congestion through the Newberg-Dundee area.

The Newberg-Dundee Bypass was built to relieve it. Phase 1, a four-mile road with one lane each way from OR 219 to OR 99W south of Dundee, opened January 6, 2018. The full bypass is planned at 11 miles and a four-lane expressway, but funding so far covers Phase 1 and design of Phase 2, per the Oregon Department of Transportation. Freight moves on the Portland & Western Railroad, and regular passenger rail ended in the 1930s.

What schools serve Newberg?

Newberg-Dundee Public Schools runs six elementary schools, two middle schools and two high schools, Newberg High School and Catalyst Alternative High School. Private Christian schools include Veritas School and C. S. Lewis Academy.

George Fox University is classed by U.S. News & World Report as a first-tier regional university, and Portland Community College runs a campus in the city.

How does Yamhill County assess property for a Newberg house?

Yamhill County values and bills Newberg property under rules set by state law. Under ORS 308.146, taxable value is the lesser of market value and a maximum assessed value that normally rises no more than 3% a year.

That cap resets when a property is new, rebuilt or substantially altered, so a house you improved or a lot that was split may be assessed differently. Taxes are due in three parts, on November 15, February 15 and May 15. A 3% discount applies to a full payment made by November 15. Ask your title company to prorate the bill at closing. Interest of 1 1/3% per month applies to late amounts, so confirm early whether any installment is still unpaid.

What about a Newberg house that is part of an estate?

Sales by court-appointed personal representatives and trustees are excluded from Oregon's seller disclosure rules under ORS 105.470. So are sales by a financial institution that took the property through foreclosure.

Other sellers of one-to-four-unit homes must provide a signed disclosure statement to each buyer who makes a written offer. If a buyer gets one, they have five business days to revoke unless they signed a waiver. Getting the right paperwork lined up first keeps an inherited sale from stalling.

How does Newberg fit into Yamhill County?

Newberg shares Yamhill County with McMinnville, Lafayette and Sheridan. The county covers 718 square miles, counted 107,722 residents in 2020, and is the fifth-smallest county in Oregon by area.

Wine is a large part of the county economy. Yamhill has more vineyard acreage than any other Oregon county, with over 80 wineries and six American Viticultural Areas wholly or partly inside its borders. Logging remains the mainstay of the western part of the county. A Newberg seller with acreage or a rural lot should ask which tax and land-use rules apply before pricing it.

What do Newberg sellers usually compare?

  • Listing with an agent versus accepting an as-is offer from a cash buyer.
  • Repair costs on an older house versus selling in present condition.
  • Closing date, tax proration and utility transfers.
  • Whether a tenant or a college renter is in the house.
  • Whether the lot is inside city limits, since city and county rules differ for rural parcels in Yamhill County.

Each buyer sets its own terms, so ask for them in writing before you decide.

Newberg is in Yamhill County, in the Portland metropolitan area. McMinnville is the county seat, and Newberg is the second most populous city in the county.
